title: Syllabus (Postgraduate)
content:
Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (Postgraduate) # Note: This syllabus outlines the plan for a 12-week, seminar-style course. Minor adjustments may be made as we progress.
Course Description # This graduate seminar is a research-oriented introduction to how adults acquire second and additional languages. We emphasize linguistic architecture, cross-linguistic variation, interfaces, processing, and implications for teaching, using Slabakova (2016) as the anchor text. Part I establishes language architecture and variation; Part II situates L2 within broader acquisition contexts and highlights the role of input; Part III surveys adult L2 morphology, syntax, the mental lexicon, interfaces, processing, and classroom implications.
Learning Objectives # By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Explain major theoretical proposals in L2 acquisition and how they derive predictions. Critically evaluate empirical studies (design, measures, analyses, interpretations). Compare acquisition across modules (morphology, syntax, lexicon) and interfaces. Relate L2 processing findings (e.g., eye-tracking, ERP) to competence and instruction. Formulate testable research questions and design a feasible study. Articulate pedagogical implications (e.g., Bottleneck Hypothesis; focus on form). Methods of Instruction # Seminar discussions, student-led paper talks, mini-methods workshops, and hands-on data critique. Expect close reading, replication thinking, and constructive debate.
Instructional Materials # Required Text # Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Oxford University Press.
(Designed for advanced undergraduates/graduate students with prior linguistics; emphasizes generative SLA and empirical methods.) Recommended (background / triangulation) # Saville-Troike, M. (2012). Introducing Second Language Acquisition (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. Selected journal articles (posted weekly). Assessment & Grading # Participation & Professionalism (10%) — consistent, informed contributions; discussants come prepared. Weekly Analytical Notes (10%) — ~300 words synthesizing key claims, predictions, and one critique. Methods/Analysis Task (20%) — short report critiquing or re-analyzing data from a published study. Seminar Lead (20%) — 30-minute critical presentation (theory, design, findings, alternatives). Final Research Proposal (40%) — 8–10 pages: motivation, literature, hypotheses, design, predicted outcomes. Total = 100%
12-Week Schedule (Topics • Chapters • Key Issues) # We read selectively and thematically; not every section of each chapter is assigned. Page-level reading lists will be posted weekly.
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Chapter: Slabakova Ch. 1
Topics: What is “knowledge of language”? Components/modules; linking theory to teachability; the scientific method in SLA (hypothesis → prediction → test).
Key issues: What counts as evidence in SLA? Property vs. transition theories.
Week 2 — Cross-Linguistic Variation & the Learning Task # Chapter: Ch. 2
Topics: Principles/parameters, Minimalist perspectives, what varies across languages, why variation matters for L2 learning.
Key issues: Initial state, transfer, setting/re-setting features; prediction and falsifiability.
Week 3 — Psychological Reality: Processing & the Parser # Chapter: Ch. 3
Topics: Processing architectures; evidence from ambiguity resolution, memory constraints, and model comparison.
Key issues: How (and when) processing interacts with grammatical knowledge; methodological cautions.
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period Debate # Chapter: Ch. 4
Topics: Age effects vs. input quality/quantity; nativelikeness; input dominance and quality.
Key issues: Operationalizing input; heritage vs. L2 learners; measuring outcomes.
Week 5 — Comparing Acquisition Contexts # Chapters: Ch. 5–6 (selected sections)
Topics: 2L1 vs. L2; child vs. adult L2; multilingualism; heritage speakers; attrition and restructuring.
Key issues: What carries over across contexts? How do context differences change predictions?
Week 6 — The Locus of Difficulty I: Functional Morphology # Chapter: Ch. 7
Topics: Morpheme studies; Missing Surface Inflection; Prosodic Transfer; Feature Reassembly.
Key issues: Why inflectional morphology is central; representation vs. performance explanations.
Week 7 — The Locus of Difficulty II: Syntax # Chapter: Ch. 8
Topics: Parameterization, word order, movement; representational deficit vs. full representation accounts.
Key issues: What “poverty of the stimulus” implies for L2 syntax; diagnostic constructions.
Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon # Chapter: Ch. 9
Topics: Bilingual lexicon models; access and inhibition; argument structure and conflation differences.
Key issues: Learning/“unlearning” mappings; negative evidence and overgeneralization.
Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface # Chapter: Ch. 10
Topics: Meaning types, mismatches, Poverty of the Stimulus in semantics, learning novel constructions.
Key issues: Where (and why) interface vulnerabilities arise; diagnostics for interface delays.
Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces # Chapter: Ch. 11
Topics: Topic/focus, pronoun reference, intonation; scalar implicatures and interface processing.
Key issues: Mapping discourse/pragmatics to form; measuring pragmatic inference in L2.
Week 11 — L2 Processing & Methods # Chapter: Ch. 12
Topics: Experimental techniques (GJT, SPR, eye-tracking, ERP); morphology & syntax in processing; individual differences.
Key issues: From competence to processing predictions; design pitfalls; effect sizes & power.
Week 12 — Teaching Implications & The Bottleneck Hypothesis # Chapter: Ch. 13
Topics: Morphology as a bottleneck; focus on form; what is hard/easy to acquire; pulling theory into practice.
Key issues: Translating evidence to pedagogy; designing theoretically motivated interventions.
Weekly Workflow (Typical) # Before class: Read assigned chapters; post Analytical Note (by 18:00 the day before). In class: 30–40 min student-led seminar; 30 min methods/data critique; 20 min synthesis. After class: Update proposal or methods task with new insights. Policies (Highlights) # Attendance & participation are essential to seminar learning. Academic integrity applies to all submissions (cite properly; no AI-generated text without disclosure and permission). Style: APA or LSA; be consistent.

title: Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science
content:
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 1: Language architecture.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # What it means to “know” a language and how this knowledge is structured into interacting modules. How SLA research adopts the scientific method: observe → generalize → hypothesize → test → revise. Why theory should make predictions (e.g., rich agreement → possible null subjects) and be falsifiable. How “teaching relevance” follows from language architecture (different modules can pose different difficulties). 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:
Define “knowledge of language” and list core modules in the architecture. Explain how the scientific method is applied in SLA and why predictions matter. Illustrate how a theoretical claim leads to a testable classroom or lab prediction. Articulate at least one teaching implication of language architecture. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 1 (Sections 1.1–1.4). Skim the “Teaching relevance” boxes embedded in Ch. 1. Guiding questions while you read:
What counts as evidence for/against a claim about L2 knowledge? Where in the architecture would you locate difficulties with e.g. agreement vs. word order? 🧠 Key terms # language architecture; module; lexicon; phonology; morphology; syntax; semantics; interfaces; hypothesis; prediction; falsifiability; null subject; transfer; Occam’s razor
🔍 Core ideas # Architecture: Language knowledge is organized into modules (lexicon, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics) that interface with sound (PF) and meaning (LF). Scientific method: Observe patterns → form hypotheses → design tests → revise models. SLA aims for explanations, not just description. Predictions: Theories must generate concrete predictions (e.g., languages with rich agreement may allow null subjects). Theory-driven SLA: Research questions stem from prior theory; outcomes support or challenge proposals. Teaching relevance: Some modules (e.g., phonology) are harder to acquire post-childhood; others (syntax, semantics) remain learnable. This shapes pedagogy. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1) # 1. What is language? What is “knowing” a language? (Ch. 1.1) # Key notes: Knowing a language involves phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic competence. Competence ≠ performance. SLA requires building an interlanguage system that maps onto these modules. Class activity: Quick discussion: which part of your L2 (sounds, word order, vocabulary) do you find most challenging? 2. The architecture of language (Ch. 1.2) # Key notes: Language is modular—phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, with interfaces. Example: adjective–noun order differs between English (“red car”) and French (“voiture rouge”). Such differences predict challenges for learners. Diagram: Instructor draws the architecture (PF ↔ Modules ↔ LF). 3. What has to be acquired in L2? (Ch. 1.3) # Key notes: Learners must re-set features not present in their L1. Example: if L1 lacks articles, learners must acquire [+definiteness] features in L2. Discussion: Is transfer always beneficial? Compare positive vs. negative transfer. 4. The scientific method in SLA (Ch. 1.4) # Key notes: SLA research is theory-driven: hypotheses must be testable and falsifiable. Example: Hypothesis—learners of Italian (rich agreement, null subject) learning English will initially drop subjects. Prediction—subject omission in early English learner data. Activity: Work in groups to formulate a simple SLA hypothesis, derive one prediction, and propose a test (e.g., grammaticality judgment). 🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2) # Goal: Practice turning a theoretical claim into a testable design.
Prompt: “If L1 allows null subjects but L2 does not, beginners may omit subjects in L2 production.”
Prediction: beginners will omit more subjects. Test: collect early learner writing/speech and compare subject use. 🧩 In-class application (Session 3) # Case vignette:
Group A: Italian L1 learners of English (null-subject language). Group B: Chinese L1 learners of English (no rich agreement).
Questions: Which group is more likely to drop subjects in early English? What evidence would falsify this prediction? What teaching intervention could target this? ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Define falsifiability and explain why it matters in SLA. Give one predicted correlation between morphology and syntax. Why are “Teaching relevance” boxes included? List the steps of the scientific method in SLA. Where in the architecture would you locate difficulty with verb movement vs. agreement endings? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due next week) # In ~300 words, (a) restate one claim from Ch. 1, (b) derive a specific prediction for L2 learners with a particular L1, and (c) propose one method to test it (e.g., GJT, self-paced reading, ERP).
🧭 Preview of Week 2 # We move from language architecture to language variation & parameters, examining how learners re-set features across languages and why this defines the SLA learning task.

title: Week 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task
content:
Week 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 2.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How languages can differ (word order, agreement, null subjects, verb movement), and what exactly an L2 learner must acquire. Principles & Parameters / Minimalist ideas: what is fixed vs. what varies; the role of features. The learning task: initial state, transfer, input “triggers,” and how learners re-set feature values. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Explain what “varies” across languages and why this matters for SLA. Describe the initial state and how transfer shapes early interlanguage. Derive testable predictions from specific cross-linguistic contrasts (e.g., null subjects, verb movement). Sketch a simple study that could detect parameter/feature re-setting in L2 learners. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 2 (read selectively with focus on: language variation, parameters, features, examples of variation, implications for learning). Optional: Revisit Ch. 1’s sections on theory → predictions → tests, as we will reuse this logic. Guiding questions:
What does it mean to “re-set” a parameter or acquire a new feature? Which kinds of input are informative (diagnostic) for learners, and which are ambiguous? 🧠 Key terms # variation; parameter; feature; micro- vs. macro-variation; transfer; initial state; positive/negative transfer; null subject; rich agreement; verb movement; headedness; triggers/cues; diagnostic evidence; ambiguity; poverty of the stimulus
🔍 Core ideas # What varies: Languages differ in how features are bundled and expressed (e.g., rich verbal agreement; placement of finite verb; availability of null subjects; head direction). Parameters & features: Under P&P/Minimalist views, universal principles hold, while feature values (and how they’re morpho-syntactically realized) vary and must be set in acquisition. Initial state & transfer: L2 learners begin with L1-based hypotheses (transfer). Early interlanguage reflects positive transfer when L1≈L2, and negative transfer when L1≠L2. The learning task: Learners rely on input cues to update feature values. Some cues are diagnostic (unambiguous), others are ambiguous and slow learning. Predictions: Cross-linguistic contrasts lead to early error signatures (e.g., subject omission in learners from null-subject L1s; misplacement of finite verbs by learners whose L1 has verb raising). 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1) # 1) What varies across languages? # Key notes: Null subjects: Italian/Spanish allow phonologically null subjects; English typically does not. Verb movement: French raises the finite verb over adverbs/negation; English generally doesn’t (auxiliaries do). Headedness/word order: VO vs. OV patterns, adjective–noun order differences. Agreement richness: Rich inflectional morphology vs. poor morphology affects syntactic options. Class activity idea: Show minimal pairs (e.g., French vs. English adverb position; Italian vs. English subjects). Students label which facts would be diagnostic for an L2 learner. 2) Principles, Parameters, and features # Key notes: Principles: Invariant properties of grammar (e.g., hierarchical structure, locality constraints). Parameters/features: Limited options whose values vary by language (e.g., [+/- null subject], presence/absence of V-to-T movement). Minimalist shift: Emphasis on features (bundling, checking, valuation) as the engine of variation. Example: If L2 has rich agreement, it may license null subjects; if L2 lacks such morphology, overt subjects are required. 3) Initial state and transfer # Key notes: Learners project L1 feature settings into L2 = transfer (often useful, sometimes misleading). Positive transfer: Similar L1-L2 settings → faster early accuracy. Negative transfer: Dissimilar settings → systematic early errors (e.g., subject drop in English by null-subject L1 learners). Discussion: Identify likely transfer outcomes for your own L1 when learning English/German/French/Chinese. 4) The learning task: input, triggers, ambiguity # Key notes: Diagnostic input: Clear evidence that forces a particular analysis (e.g., overt expletive “it” in English with weather verbs). Ambiguous input: Compatible with multiple grammars → slower updating. Prediction: Learning trajectories depend on frequency and diagnosticity of cues. Activity: In groups, take one contrast (e.g., verb movement). Propose a single sentence pattern that would be maximally diagnostic for learners. 🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2) # Goal: Turn a cross-linguistic contrast into a testable design.
Prompt: Choose one contrast and derive a prediction + method.
Contrast A (Null subject): L1 Italian → L2 English.
Prediction: Higher subject omission in early L2 English production by Italian L1 learners vs. Chinese L1 learners. Method: Elicited narrative or learner corpus analysis; code rate of overt vs. null subjects. Contrast B (Verb movement): L1 French → L2 English.
Prediction: Misplacement of finite verb around adverbs/negation in early L2 English. Method: Acceptability Judgement Task (AJT) or Elicited Imitation contrasting often position (e.g., “John often eats sushi” vs. “John eats often sushi”). Contrast C (Headedness): L1 Japanese (OV) → L2 English (VO).
Prediction: Early word-order errors in complex VPs; slower convergence where input is ambiguous. Method: Self-Paced Reading (SPR) with regions that disambiguate verb–object order. 🧩 In-class application (Session 3) # Case vignette:
Group A: Spanish L1 learners of English (rich agreement, null subject). Group B: Mandarin L1 learners of English (no rich agreement, no null subject parameter).
Questions: Which group will initially omit subjects more in English? Why? What data pattern would falsify this prediction? Design one classroom task that supplies diagnostic evidence for the target setting. ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Define transfer and give one example of negative transfer relevant to Ch. 2. What is a parameter/feature value? Provide one case that differs across languages. Why is diagnostic input important for the learning task? State one testable prediction about verb movement for L1 French → L2 English. How do rich agreement systems relate to null subjects in theoretical predictions? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 3) # In ~300 words, pick one contrast (null subject, verb movement, or headedness). (a) State the theoretical claim, (b) derive a prediction for learners with a specific L1, and (c) outline one method (task + measure) that could detect change over time.
🧭 Preview of Week 3 # We move from “what varies” to processing models: how the L2 parser works, and how processing constraints shape the path from competence to performance.

title: Week 3 — Processing & the Parser: How L2 is Used in Real Time
content:
Week 3 — Processing & the Parser: How L2 is Used in Real Time # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 3.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How the mind parses language incrementally and what this implies for second language (L2) comprehension and production. Core processing architectures and why performance sometimes diverges from grammatical competence. What L2 processing predicts for error signatures, reaction times, and eye-movement patterns, and how methods can detect them. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Explain how incremental parsing builds structure on the fly and where garden-paths come from. Distinguish competence vs. performance explanations for L2 behavior. Describe key processing models (e.g., cue-based retrieval; good-enough processing) and their L2 predictions. Propose a testable design (e.g., SPR, eye-tracking, ERP) linking a processing claim to measurable outcomes. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 3 (focus on: processing architectures; ambiguity resolution; memory limitations; predictions for L2). Optional: Skim the methodological overviews in Ch. 12 to preview tools we’ll use later (GJT, SPR, eye-tracking, ERP). Guiding questions:
Why does incremental interpretation sometimes lead to misanalysis? What would count as evidence that a difficulty is processing-based rather than representational? 🧠 Key terms # incremental parsing; garden-path; ambiguity resolution; reanalysis; cue-based retrieval; similarity-based interference; working memory; local vs. structural distance; good-enough processing; surprisal; speed–accuracy trade-off; offline vs. online measures
🔍 Core ideas # Incrementality: The parser commits early to a structure based on probabilistic cues; strong priors can mislead (garden-paths) and require reanalysis. Competence vs. performance: A learner may know a structure (competence) yet still read it more slowly or err under time pressure (performance). Cue-based retrieval: Integration depends on retrieving the correct dependency from memory; interference occurs when distractors share features (e.g., number). Good-enough processing: Under load, the system may settle for plausible representations without full detail, increasing shallow-structure outcomes. Measurement matters: Online methods (SPR, eye-tracking, ERP) detect time-course effects that offline accuracy may miss. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1) # 1) What does the parser do, and when? # Key notes: Parsing is incremental—word-by-word commitments; ambiguity is resolved using lexical, syntactic, and discourse cues. Early commitments can create garden-paths (e.g., “While Anna dressed the baby…”) requiring reanalysis. Class activity idea: Read classic garden-path sentences aloud; predict where reanalysis will occur and why. 2) Sources of difficulty: ambiguity & memory # Key notes: Ambiguities (attachment, filler–gap, relative clauses) and memory constraints drive slowdowns. Long dependencies and structural complexity increase retrieval demands. Example: Subject vs. object relative clauses; the object relatives often incur larger integration costs, especially for L2 readers. 3) Cue-based retrieval & interference # Key notes: The system retrieves earlier material by matching features (e.g., number, gender). Similarity-based interference (distractors share features) produces slowdowns or attraction errors (e.g., “The key to the cabinets are…”). Discussion: Predict which L1→L2 pairings heighten interference for agreement dependencies. 4) Competence vs. performance: L2 implications # Key notes: Slower or less accurate online performance does not imply lack of competence. Processing load, not representational deficit, can explain delayed or shallow effects—especially under time pressure. Activity: For a phenomenon you know (e.g., verb movement or agreement), sketch both a competence account and a processing account. What data would differentiate them? 🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2) # Goal: Link a processing claim to an empirical signature.
Choose one design and complete the template.
Self-Paced Reading (SPR)
Claim: L2 readers experience interference in long-distance agreement. Prediction: Longer reading times at the agreement region when a distractor noun mismatches the subject’s number. Measure: Region-by-region RTs; compare match vs. mismatch conditions. Eye-tracking during Reading
Claim: L2 readers show extended regressions in garden-paths. Prediction: Increased first-pass and regression-path times at the disambiguating region. Measure: First fixation, gaze duration, regression path, total time. ERP
Claim: L2 detects morpho-syntactic violations but with delayed/attenuated responses. Prediction: P600 modulation for agreement violations; latency/amplitude differences vs. L1. Measure: Component amplitude/latency windows; artifact rejection; item-level averaging. 🧩 In-class application (Session 3) # Case vignette: Agreement attraction in L2 English
Sentence frame: “The key to the cabinets are/is on the table.”
Questions: What interference pattern do you predict for L1s with rich agreement vs. poor agreement systems? If offline accuracy is native-like but online times show large slowdowns, what does that imply? Propose one instructional activity that targets agreement dependencies under processing load. ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Why do garden-path sentences cause slowdowns? Define similarity-based interference in cue-based retrieval. Give one reason online measures can diverge from offline accuracy in L2. What pattern would support a processing (not competence) account for an L2 difficulty? Name one ERP component associated with morpho-syntactic violations and its interpretation. 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 4) # In ~300 words, pick one phenomenon (garden-paths, agreement attraction, or relative clause attachment). (a) State a processing-based claim, (b) derive a time-course prediction (which region/measure), and (c) choose a method (SPR, eye-tracking, or ERP) with one analytic decision you would preregister.
🧭 Preview of Week 4 # We shift to age effects, input quality/quantity, and the Critical Period—how biological constraints and the distribution of input shape L2 outcomes and what counts as convincing evidence.

title: Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period
content:
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 4.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # What Critical/Sensitive Period claims predict for L2 acquisition and how these claims are tested. How input quantity and quality shape outcomes — sometimes more than age — and how to disentangle their effects. Why conclusions hinge on measurement choices (global accent vs. fine-grained morphosyntax) and design controls (AoA, LoR, education, use, dominance). 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Define Critical/Sensitive Period hypotheses for L2 and state their testable predictions. Explain how input quantity/quality and experience (LoR, use, education) confound or moderate age effects. Evaluate evidence for/against age effects based on what is measured (phonology vs. morphosyntax vs. semantics/pragmatics). Design a feasible study that separates age and input influences and identifies appropriate outcome measures. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 4 (Age effects, input quantity/quality, “nativelikeness,” methodological caveats). Optional: Skim Ch. 12’s brief overviews of methods to anticipate Week 11. Guiding questions:
What, exactly, would count as falsifying a strong Critical Period claim? Which measures are most sensitive to age (accent? inflectional morphology? lexical semantics?) and why? 🧠 Key terms # Critical Period (CPH); Sensitive period; Age of Arrival (AoA); Length of Residence (LoR); ultimate attainment; nativelikeness; input quantity; input quality; dominance; literacy/education; diagnostic evidence; confound; moderation; global vs. local measures
🔍 Core ideas # Not one outcome, many: Age relates differently to phonology (large age effects), morphosyntax (mixed), and semantics/pragmatics (often learnable with input). Input matters: The amount (quantity) and informativeness (quality/diagnosticity) of input can attenuate age effects; poor or ambiguous input slows attainment. Operationalization is destiny: “Nativelikeness” depends on what you measure (accent ≠ grammar ≠ processing). Global ratings and local diagnostics can diverge. Design before verdict: Strong claims (e.g., maturational closing) require controls for use, education, SES, literacy, motivation, and task demands. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) What do Critical/Sensitive Period claims predict? # Key notes: Strong CPH: maturational window closes → discontinuity in outcomes by AoA. Sensitive period: continuous decline with age, but learning remains possible. Predictions: later AoA → lower ultimate attainment holding input constant; the shape (break vs. slope) is empirical. Class spark: One-minute write: Which skill in your L2 feels most “age-locked”? Why? 2) Evidence patterns & measurement choices # Key notes: Phonology typically shows robust age effects; morphosyntax shows mixed results depending on measure (accuracy vs. online processing). Global vs. local: “Sounds native” ≠ “uses inflection/article semantics native-like.” Task effects: time pressure (online) reveals processing costs despite near-native offline accuracy. Think–pair–share: Identify a study conclusion that would flip if a different measure were used. 3) Input quantity/quality and design controls # Key notes: Quantity (hours/years, richness of exposure) and quality (diagnostic cues, literacy, classroom focus on form) can mediate age effects. Control for LoR, current use, education, and dominance; report exposure profiles. Quick design pitch: In pairs, propose one control you’d add to an AoA study and say why it matters. Pacing note: Three topics x ~12 min each + 9 min discussion fits a 45-min session.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Separate age from input in a simple, testable design.
Define outcome (choose ONE):
Global accent rating • inflectional morphology accuracy • article semantics • scalar implicature judgments. Groups (match on input where possible):
Early/AoA≤7 vs. Late/AoA≥15; match LoR, current L2 use, education. Prediction (pick the right shape):
Discontinuity at a boundary (strong CPH) or gradual slope (sensitive period). Specify which module should show the effect (e.g., phonology > morphosyntax). Measures & controls:
Outcome measure + at least two covariates (LoR, use, literacy). Plan power (rough N) and analysis (e.g., regression with AoA, covariates). Report (2–3 lines):
Hypothesis, key prediction, primary measure, and what result would falsify your claim. 🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette (small-group analysis → whole-class synthesis)
Group A: AoA 18, LoR 12 yrs, daily L2 use at work, high literacy; Outcome: near-native morphosyntax online but accented speech. Group B: AoA 9, LoR 12 yrs, low L2 use, limited literacy; Outcome: native-like accent but unstable article semantics. Questions:
Which results follow CPH expectations, and which highlight input effects? What additional data would you collect to adjudicate? Design one teaching intervention targeting the weaker domain in each group (focus on form? input enhancement? tasks?). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # State one falsifiable prediction of a strong CPH for L2. Give an example where measure choice changes the age conclusion. Define input quality and give a diagnostic example. Name two covariates that must be controlled in AoA studies. What result would favor a sensitive-period over a strict CPH? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 5) # In ~300 words, choose one outcome domain (phonology, morphosyntax, or semantics/pragmatics). (a) State a CPH or sensitive-period claim for that domain, (b) derive a prediction that controls for input/use, and (c) outline a measure + analysis (variables, covariates, expected pattern).
🧭 Preview of Week 5 # We compare acquisition contexts — simultaneous bilinguals, early L2, adult L2, heritage speakers, attrition — and ask what transfers, what restructures, and how context reshapes predictions.

title: Week 5 — Comparing Acquisition Contexts: 2L1, Adult L2, Heritage & Attrition
content:
Week 5 — Comparing Acquisition Contexts: 2L1, Adult L2, Heritage & Attrition # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Ch. 5–6 (selected).
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How acquisition context (simultaneous bilingualism/2L1, sequential/Adult L2, Heritage, Attrition) shapes the path and outcomes of acquisition. What transfers, what restructures, and how input timing/amount/quality and dominance shift predictions. Practical takeaways for designing studies and targeted instruction in each group. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Distinguish 2L1, Adult L2, Heritage, and Attrition profiles and state group-specific predictions for morphology, syntax, and interfaces. Explain how input timing/quality and language dominance mediate similarities/differences across groups. Evaluate whether a pattern reflects incomplete acquisition, attrition, or processing pressure. Sketch a controlled comparison (groups, property, task, covariates) that can adjudicate between explanations. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 5–6 (selected)
Focus your notes on: (i) 2L1 vs. Adult L2 contrasts, (ii) Heritage acquisition profiles and dominance, (iii) Attrition vs. incomplete acquisition, (iv) Illustrative morpho-syntactic phenomena. Optional: Revisit Ch. 3–4 highlights (processing, age/input) for links to Week 5. Guiding questions:
Which properties are most likely to differ across contexts (e.g., functional morphology, clitic placement, subject expression, gender/CASE, articles/definiteness), and why? How would you tell incomplete acquisition apart from attrition using design and measures? 🧠 Key terms # 2L1 / simultaneous bilingualism; sequential bilingualism; Adult L2; Heritage language; dominance; input timing/quality; incomplete acquisition; attrition; restructuring; crosslinguistic influence; stabilization; ultimate attainment; interfaces (syntax–semantics/pragmatics).
🔍 Core ideas # Context matters: 2L1 receives early, rich, balanced input in both languages; Adult L2 begins late, often classroom-heavy; Heritage learners have early naturalistic input but later reduced input and dominance shift; Attriters show loss/weakening tied to reduced use. Predicted strengths/weaknesses: 2L1: native-like developmental path; occasional crosslinguistic influence but robust end-state when input is sufficient. Adult L2: vulnerabilities in functional morphology and some interfaces; stronger role for transfer and processing pressure. Heritage: strong phonology/lexicon; selective vulnerabilities in morphology and discourse-conditioned syntax (e.g., subject expression, clitics) due to input profile. Attrition: erosion in low-frequency/late-acquired morpho-syntax and discourse mapping, especially under limited use. Diagnosing source: Distinguish incomplete acquisition (never fully robust) vs. attrition (previously acquired, later weakened) via age-of-onset, input history, use, and change over time. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Mapping the contexts: who acquires what, when? # Key notes: 2L1 vs. Adult L2 vs. Heritage vs. Attrition; typical AoO, input type, domains of strength/weakness; role of dominance. Class spark: Quick poll—Which group would you expect to outperform in phonology, functional morphology, interface pragmatics, and processing speed? Why? 2) Group-specific predictions by domain # Key notes: Functional morphology (agreement, tense/aspect, gender/CASE): Adult L2 & Heritage often show selective instability; 2L1 less so with balanced input. Syntax (movement, clitic placement): Adult L2 may show transfer-shaped errors; Heritage may show optional forms tied to discourse routines. Interfaces (syntax–semantics/pragmatics): Heritage and Adult L2 can lag where discourse cues are sparse in input. Example: Subject expression (null vs. overt) and clitics in Romance; articles/definiteness in English; gender agreement in Spanish. 3) Incomplete acquisition vs. attrition: design and evidence # Key notes: Incomplete acquisition: property never stabilized (traceable to early input profile). Attrition: previously stabilized but erodes with reduced use. Use history, longitudinal or age-stratified designs, and task contrasts (online vs. offline) to diagnose. Think–pair–share: For “gender agreement in Heritage Spanish,” list two patterns that would imply incomplete acquisition vs. attrition. 🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Build a compact study that cleanly compares two contexts on one property.
Choose a property (one only):
(A) Gender agreement (Spanish); (B) Object clitic placement (Romance); (C) Subject expression (null vs. overt); (D) English article definiteness. Pick two groups (match on age now, SES, and education where possible):
2L1 vs. Adult L2 • 2L1 vs. Heritage • Heritage vs. Adult L2 • Heritage vs. Attrition. State a prediction (direction + rationale):
e.g., Heritage < 2L1 in gender agreement accuracy but Heritage ≈ 2L1 in lexical access. Method & measures (one task, one primary DV + one control DV):
AJT (accuracy + RT), elicited production (error rates), SPR (region RTs), or eye-tracking (gaze/first-pass/total time). Include covariates: current use, dominance, education, proficiency. Adjudication: What outcome would indicate incomplete acquisition vs. attrition vs. processing pressure?
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette (triad comparison)
Group A (2L1 Spanish-English): balanced early input; high current use both languages. Group B (Heritage Spanish): early Spanish at home, schooling in English; low current Spanish use. Group C (Adult L2 Spanish): English L1, late classroom exposure to Spanish; high motivation. Task: Object clitics and subject expression
Predict accuracy and RT orderings across the three groups. Identify which pattern would falsify “incomplete acquisition” for Group B and instead support attrition or processing. Propose one instructional focus per group (e.g., input enhancement for clitics; discourse-linked practice for subject expression). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Give one strength and one vulnerability typically associated with Heritage grammars. How would you distinguish incomplete acquisition from attrition in study design? Name two covariates that must be controlled when comparing 2L1 vs. Heritage outcomes. Which domain is most likely to show group differences across contexts and why? Give one falsifiable prediction contrasting Adult L2 vs. 2L1 for gender agreement. 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 6) # In ~300 words, select one property and two groups (e.g., Heritage vs. Adult L2). (a) State a theory-based prediction, (b) specify one task + primary DV, (c) list two covariates you will control, and (d) say what outcome would imply incomplete acquisition vs. attrition vs. processing.
🧭 Preview of Week 6 # We zoom into the locus of difficulty in functional morphology—why inflectional morphology is often fragile in L2/heritage grammars and how to test Feature Reassembly vs. performance accounts.

title: Week 6 — Functional Morphology: Where (and Why) L2 Morphology Is Fragile
content:
Week 6 — Functional Morphology: Where (and Why) L2 Morphology Is Fragile # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 7.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # Why inflectional morphology (tense, agreement, case, gender) is often the locus of difficulty in L2 and heritage grammars. Competing explanations: representation (features not fully acquired/reassembled) vs. performance (surface realization problems, prosodic/mapping issues). Practical tools to test these views with targeted contrasts and diagnostic tasks. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Describe classic accounts of L2 morphological variability (e.g., Missing Surface Inflection, Prosodic Transfer, Feature Reassembly). Distinguish representation vs. performance/mapping explanations and derive testable predictions. Identify diagnostic properties (e.g., agreement vs. tense; gender vs. case) for designing compact studies. Propose a feasible method (AJT, elicited production, priming, SPR) that isolates feature representation from surface form realization. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 7 (focus on: morphological variability; MSIH; PTH; Feature Reassembly; comprehension–production asymmetries). Optional: Revisit Ch. 3 (processing) to link online timing to morphological decisions. Guiding questions:
If a learner understands tense/agreement in comprehension but omits inflection in production, what does that imply? What counts as evidence that a feature has been (re)assembled vs. only surface-marked? 🧠 Key terms # inflectional morphology; agreement; tense/aspect; case; gender; Missing Surface Inflection Hypothesis (MSIH); Prosodic Transfer Hypothesis (PTH); Feature Reassembly Hypothesis (FRH); realization vs. representation; mapping; optionality; comprehension–production asymmetry; priming.
🔍 Core ideas # Variability ≠ ignorance: Learners can know a feature (e.g., 3sg agreement) yet omit or mis-realize its surface exponent under pressure. MSIH: Representations are intact; variability is at the spell-out/phonological mapping stage → predicts better comprehension than production. PTH: L1 prosodic templates affect where/when morphology can surface → predicts position-specific or syllable/foot-sensitive omissions. Feature Reassembly (FRH): L2 requires reconfiguring features and their bundling (e.g., definiteness, number, gender) → predicts asymmetric success across features and languages, even with the same “category label.” Diagnostics: Contrast form-identical vs. feature-identical items; compare comprehension (AJT, priming) vs. production (elicitation) to locate the bottleneck. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) What “lives” in morphology and why it’s hard # Key notes: Agreement (person/number), tense/aspect, case, gender—small forms, big feature load; low perceptual salience; late-acquired and low-frequency combinations are especially vulnerable. Class spark: 2-minute poll—Which morphology caused you most trouble in an L2 (and in what context)? 2) Three explanations for variability # MSIH (surface realization bottleneck) Prediction: Near-native interpretation of tense/agreement contrasts; omissions/mis-formations in production—especially under speed/complexity. PTH (prosodic constraints on realization) Prediction: Omissions tied to prosodic position (e.g., word-final weak syllables) or clitic placement patterns; improvement when prosody favors overt marking. FRH (feature (re)mapping) Prediction: Difficulty where L2 requires new feature bundles or different feature–form mappings (e.g., gender on determiners/adjectives; article definiteness for bare-N languages). 3) How to tell them apart (design heuristics) # Key notes: Comprehension vs. production asymmetry → favors MSIH. Position/syllable effects → favors PTH. Feature-specific cross-language asymmetries (same form, different features) → favors FRH. Quick demo: Judge vs. produce minimal pairs for 3sg -s, past -ed, or gender agreement; note where breakdown occurs. Pacing: Three focused mini-sections (~12 min each) + 9 min guided discussion.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Build a discriminating test that can separate MSIH, PTH, and FRH accounts.
Pick one domain (one only):
(A) 3sg agreement in English, (B) past tense -ed, (C) gender agreement (Spanish), or (D) case marking (German). Contrast two tasks (to locate the bottleneck):
Comprehension: AJT with minimal pairs or morphological priming (facilitation when features match). Production: Elicited production under time pressure vs. no time pressure. Add a prosody manipulation (if relevant):
Strong vs. weak final syllables; clitic position; stress pattern changes. Predictions:
MSIH → intact comprehension, variable production, bigger time-pressure effect. PTH → position-sensitive omissions; prosody tweak reduces errors. FRH → selective difficulty tied to feature bundles (e.g., gender+number), even when prosody/time are controlled. Output: 3-line prereg summary: hypothesis, primary DV (accuracy/RT/priming), and falsifier.
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette: English 3sg -s & Spanish gender
Group A (L1 Mandarin → L2 English): high comprehension of subject–verb agreement contrasts; frequent 3sg -s omissions in spontaneous speech. Group B (L1 English → L2 Spanish): good lexical gender knowledge but inconsistent adjective agreement and determiner–noun concord. Questions:
Which pattern points to MSIH vs. FRH, and why? What prosodic tweak might help Group A (if any)? Design one classroom activity for each group that targets the hypothesized bottleneck (e.g., input enhancement for feature bundles; rhythmic production drills for prosody). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # What empirical pattern would support MSIH over FRH? Give one prediction unique to PTH. What would count as evidence for Feature Reassembly? Why include priming in morphology studies? Name one design move that separates representation from realization. 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 7) # In ~300 words, choose one domain (agreement, past tense, gender, or case). (a) State whether you predict MSIH, PTH, or FRH to best explain early variability; (b) give one prediction for comprehension vs. production (and/or prosody); (c) propose one task and one falsifier.
🧭 Preview of Week 7 # We move from morphology to syntax: word order and movement, and how to diagnose representational vs. processing explanations in clause-structure phenomena.

title: Week 7 — Syntax: Word Order, Movement, and Competing Accounts
content:
Week 7 — Syntax: Word Order, Movement, and Competing Accounts # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 8.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How syntactic movement and word-order properties (e.g., V-to-T, V2, head direction) create specific challenges in L2 acquisition. What long-distance dependencies (wh-movement, relative clauses, islands) reveal about L2 grammatical representations. How to adjudicate between representational accounts (e.g., failed/feature deficits, full transfer/full access) and processing accounts (e.g., shallow structure under time pressure). 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Explain core diagnostics for verb placement (V-to-T, V2) and wh-movement, and derive L1-specific predictions. Distinguish A- vs. A′-movement, and identify island configurations in experimental materials. Contrast representational deficit (e.g., failed functional features) vs. full representation + processing (e.g., shallow structure) hypotheses with testable predictions. Propose a compact experiment or elicitation task to probe a syntactic property with clear outcome measures. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 8 (focus: verb movement/word order, long-distance dependencies, major theoretical accounts and their predictions). Optional: Revisit Ch. 3 (processing) for links between online measures and syntactic effects. Guiding questions:
Which minimal pairs best diagnose V-to-T or V2? What would count as evidence for or against a representational deficit (vs. a processing limitation) in L2 syntax? 🧠 Key terms # V-to-T movement; V2 (verb-second); head direction(ality); A-movement vs. A′-movement; wh-movement; islands (wh-island, complex NP, subject island); EPP; feature checking/valuation; Full Transfer/Full Access (FT/FA); Failed Functional Features / Representational Deficit; Shallow Structure Hypothesis (SSH); optionality; embedded vs. main clause contrasts.
🔍 Core ideas # Movement & placement: Many word-order differences (adverb/negation position, subject–aux inversion, clause-final verbs) are movement-driven; learners’ L1 settings predict early placement errors. Dependencies & constraints: Wh-movement and relative clauses create filler–gap dependencies; islands constrain movement—use these to test whether L2 grammars encode abstract constraints. Competing accounts: Representational deficit: Certain functional features (e.g., strong movement triggers) are absent or unrecoverable → persistent optionality even with time/practice. Full representation + processing (e.g., SSH): Target-like features are present, but time pressure or memory load yields shallower online structure-building, leading to slower RTs or more errors under speed. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Word order & movement diagnostics (V-to-T, V2, head direction) # Key notes: V-to-T: French allows finite verbs to appear before adverbs/negation (V raises), English typically doesn’t (finite main verbs stay below Adv/Neg; auxiliaries move). V2: Germanic V2 puts the finite verb in second position in main clauses (not the same in embedded clauses). Head direction: OV vs. VO / head-final vs. head-initial affects verb–object order and placement of particles/clauses. Class activity: Label the diagnostic region in minimal pairs (e.g., Jean (souvent) mange des pommes vs. John often eats apples / John eats often apples). 2) Long-distance dependencies (wh, relatives) & island constraints # Key notes: A′-movement (wh/fronting) vs. A-movement (passive/raising). Islands: wh-island (embedded Q), complex NP (relative clauses / complements of nouns), subject islands. Use island violations to ask if L2 grammars respect abstract constraints (competence) even if online reanalysis is costly. Example: Compare acceptability for wh-extraction from complements vs. from island positions. 3) Competing accounts & predictions (deficit vs. processing) # Key notes: Deficit/failed features → persistent misplacement or acceptance of ungrammatical extraction even in untimed, highly explicit tasks. Full representation + processing → native-like judgments in untimed tasks but slower RTs / more regressions in online tasks, especially in complex environments. Quick demo: Untimed AJT vs. timed AJT on the same contrasts—predict which differences will surface only under time pressure. Pacing: Three focused segments (~12 min each) + ~9 min discussion on where your L1 would create the strongest predictions.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Design a compact test for one syntactic property that distinguishes representation from processing explanations.
Pick ONE property and complete the template:
Property A — V-to-T (adverb/negation placement)
Groups: L1 French vs. L1 Mandarin → L2 English (matched proficiency). Task: AJT + SPR on adverb placement (e.g., often position). Predictions: Deficit → persistent acceptance of John eats often sushi in AJT + limited improvement. Processing → native-like AJT but longer RTs at adverb region in SPR for the disallowed order. Property B — V2 (main vs. embedded clauses)
Groups: L1 German vs. L1 Mandarin → L2 English. Task: Elicited production of declaratives/questions + AJT on embedded inversion. Predictions: Deficit → continued overuse of inversion in embedded clauses in both tasks. Processing → correct judgments offline, occasional production slips under speed/complexity. Property C — Wh-movement & islands
Groups: L1 Mandarin (wh-in-situ) vs. L1 Spanish (wh-fronting) → L2 English. Task: AJT (grammatical vs. island violations) + Eye-tracking on wh-dependencies. Predictions: Deficit → acceptance of island extractions even in untimed AJT. Processing → reject island violations offline but show prolonged regressions/slowdowns at gap or disambiguation online. Deliverable: 3-line prereg: hypothesis, primary DV (accuracy/acceptability, RTs, regressions), and falsifier.
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette
Group A: L1 French → L2 English. Accurate on auxiliaries, but variable finite main-verb placement with adverbs in timed production. Group B: L1 Mandarin → L2 English. Rejects wh-island violations in AJT, but shows large regression-path times at island boundaries. Questions:
Which pattern points to processing vs. representational explanations, and why? What additional control (e.g., proficiency matching, working-memory screening) would you add to sharpen the inference? Propose one teaching activity per group (e.g., adverb-placement drills with timed speaking; structured reading tasks highlighting island boundaries). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Give one minimal pair that diagnoses V-to-T in English vs. French. What is an island, and why is it useful in L2 testing? What outcome supports a processing (not deficit) account for wh-movement? One prediction for V2 transfer into L2 English. How do you separate representation from real-time performance in design? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 8) # In ~300 words, choose one property (V-to-T, V2, or wh/islands). (a) State a deficit and a processing prediction, (b) propose one task with a primary DV, and (c) specify a falsifier for your preferred account.
🧭 Preview of Week 8 # Next we turn to the mental lexicon—representation, access/inhibition, and how lexical–argument structure mappings are acquired and processed in L2.

title: Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon: Representation, Access, and Argument Structure
content:
Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon: Representation, Access, and Argument Structure # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 9.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How the bilingual mental lexicon is organized and accessed in real time: cross-language activation, inhibition, cognate/false-friend effects. What L2 learners must acquire beyond word form and core meaning: feature bundles, morphological decomposition, collocations, and argument-structure mappings. How to test lexical representation and access with lexical decision, (masked) priming, picture naming, and eye-tracking/ERP. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Describe major models of the bilingual lexicon and predict patterns for cognates, interlingual homographs, and translation equivalents. Explain cross-language activation and inhibition and how they show up in RTs, accuracy, and priming. Distinguish form, lemma-level (syntactic/semantic), and morphological representations; predict when decomposition facilitates or hinders L2 processing. Explain argument-structure and subcategorization learning (e.g., which verbs take which complements) and design a compact test of lexical–syntactic mapping. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 9 (focus on: bilingual lexicon models, lexical access/inhibition, cognates & homographs, morphological decomposition, argument structure). Optional: Revisit Ch. 3 (processing) for methods links and time-course interpretations. Guiding questions:
Why do cognates often help but interlingual homographs can hurt performance? How do learners acquire which complements a verb licenses (e.g., explain something to someone vs. discuss about)? 🧠 Key terms # bilingual lexicon; cross-language activation; inhibition; cognate; interlingual homograph; translation asymmetry; lemma; subcategorization frame; argument structure; morphological decomposition; derivational vs. inflectional morphology; lexical decision; masked priming; picture naming; N400; frequency/AoA effects; collocation.
🔍 Core ideas # Nonselective access: Both languages are co-activated; the L2 user must inhibit the non-target language—predicts cognate facilitation and homograph interference. Levels of representation: Form (orthography/phonology) Lemma (syntactic/semantic info; subcategorization, argument structure) Morphology (decomposition: stems + affixes; feature bundles). Morphology & the lexicon: L2 readers may decompose reliably for frequent/transparent affixes but show costs for opaque or low-frequency forms. Argument structure learning: Beyond meanings of words, learners must map who does what to whom (frames and complements). Negative transfer yields errors like discuss about or misusing causative/inchoative alternations. Methods matter: Lexical decision and masked priming capture early form/lemma activation; picture naming taps production; N400 modulations and eye-tracking show time-course of lexical–semantic integration. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Models & predictions of the bilingual lexicon # Key notes: Lexical access is largely nonselective; L1 and L2 compete/cooperate. Expect cognate speed-ups, homograph slowdowns, and translation asymmetries (L2→L1 often easier than L1→L2 early on). Class spark: Elicit quick examples of cognates and false friends from students’ languages; predict RT/accuracy effects. 2) Representation levels & morphological decomposition # Key notes: Separate form knowledge from lemma (subcategorization, semantic selection) and morphology (stems/affixes). Transparency and frequency modulate decomposition; derivational morphology may be harder than inflectional in L2 reading. Micro-demo: Show pairs like teacher–teach, happiness–happy, government–govern; ask which are likely decomposed online by L2 readers and why. 3) Argument structure & subcategorization # Key notes: Learners must acquire verb-specific frames (e.g., depend on X, remind NP of NP), event-structure mappings (causative/inchoative), and prepositional selection. Transfer predicts specific error signatures. Think–pair–share: For three verbs (explain, discuss, provide), list the correct frames and the most likely L1-based errors. Pacing: ~12 min per mini-topic + ~9 min discussion fits the 45-min block.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Connect a theoretical claim to a diagnostic task and measure.
Choose one focus and complete the template.
A. Cognates vs. homographs (nonselective access)
Claim: Cross-language activation boosts cognates but harms homographs. Task: Masked priming lexical decision (prime: L1 or L2; target: cognate/homograph/noncognate). Prediction: Faster RTs for cognates; slower or less accurate for homographs; priming across languages. B. Morphological decomposition
Claim: Transparent affixes support decomposition; opaque/low-frequency forms reduce it. Task: Lexical decision with morphological primes (stem/affix) vs. orthographic controls. Prediction: Larger priming for transparent derivations/inflections; reduced/absent priming for opaque pairs. C. Argument structure frames
Claim: L2 learners undergeneralize/overgeneralize verb frames until frames are learned. Task: Acceptability judgment on subcategorization (e.g., discuss about, explain to, provide with), plus SPR for processing cost. Prediction: Offline acceptance improves with proficiency; online costs linger at preposition/complement region. Deliverable: 3-line prereg—hypothesis, primary DV (RT, accuracy, N400 amplitude), and falsifier.
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette
Group A (Spanish L1 → English): strong cognate facilitation; occasional false-friend errors (actual vs. actualmente). Group B (Chinese L1 → English): slower derivational morphology; difficulty with argument-structure for certain verbs (provide X with Y). Questions:
Which patterns reflect nonselective access vs. representation gaps at the lemma or morphology level? What design tweak would isolate inhibition costs (e.g., language-switching blocks)? Propose one teaching intervention per group (e.g., collocation/phrase-frame drills; contrastive lists of false friends with usage contexts). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Why do cognates often show faster RTs while interlingual homographs can slow readers down? What evidence suggests morphological decomposition in L2 readers? Give one example of a subcategorization error and the frame it violates. How would you detect inhibition in bilingual access? What pattern would indicate a lemma-level (not just form-level) learning effect? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 9) # In ~300 words, pick one target (cognates/homographs, morphological decomposition, or argument structure). (a) State a claim, (b) derive a prediction (who/when/where in the sentence), (c) choose one task + DV, and (d) specify a falsifier.
🧭 Preview of Week 9 # We move to the syntax–semantics interface: when meaning composition and syntactic structure mismatch, and why certain semantic distinctions are especially hard in L2.

title: Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface: Meaning Composition, Telicity, and Scope
content:
Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface: Meaning Composition, Telicity, and Scope # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 10.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How syntactic structure and semantic composition interact to yield meanings (event types, definiteness/specificity, scope). Why L2 learners struggle with telicity/aspect, article semantics, and quantifier scope—and what this predicts for data patterns. Minimal, testable designs for the interface: truth-value judgment, acceptability with controlled contexts, and online measures. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Explain how event structure (state, activity, accomplishment, achievement) and object quantization affect telicity. Distinguish definiteness vs. specificity and predict article-use challenges for learners from article-less L1s. Describe scope ambiguities and derive L1-specific predictions for inverse scope in L2. Propose a compact experiment (materials, context, DV) that targets a syntax–semantics interface contrast. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 10 (focus on: compositionality; event semantics & telicity; article semantics: definiteness/specificity/genericity; quantifiers & scope). Optional: Revisit Ch. 8 (syntax diagnostics) and Ch. 3 (processing) for links to structure and time-course. Guiding questions:
Why does eat apples pattern differently from eat an apple or eat the apple in aspectual interpretation? How can the same surface sentence have two truth conditions (scope ambiguity), and how would you test which reading a learner has? 🧠 Key terms # compositionality; event structure (state/activity/accomplishment/achievement); telicity; quantization vs. cumulativity; perfective vs. imperfective; article semantics; definiteness; specificity; genericity; quantifiers; scope; inverse scope; distributive vs. collective; truth-value judgment task (TVJT).
🔍 Core ideas # Event composition & telicity: VP meaning arises from verb + object; quantized objects (e.g., an apple, three apples) tend to yield telic interpretations (bounded events), while mass/plural bare objects (apples, rice) favor atelic readings. Articles & DP features: Languages package [±definite], [±specific], and generic readings differently. Learners from article-less L1s must map new features to forms; expect overuse/underuse of the/a and confusion in context-dependent readings. Quantification & scope: Sentences with multiple quantifiers (e.g., A student read every book) can have surface (∃ > ∀) and inverse (∀ > ∃) readings. L1 grammar and processing preferences shape which readings L2 learners access. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Event structure & telicity # Key notes: Accomplishments (bounded events) vs. activities (unbounded) depend on the internal argument: eat an apple (telic) vs. eat apples (atelic). Adding measure phrases (drink a glass of water) or resultative structure increases boundedness. Predictions: Learners may misinterpret aspect when the object’s quantization or measure is the only cue. Class spark: Label a set of VPs (provided) as telic/atelic and justify by object type/measure. 2) Article semantics: definiteness, specificity, generics # Key notes: Definiteness = unique, familiar referent (the book); specificity = speaker intends a particular but not necessarily familiar referent (a certain book). Generics: The tiger/The tigers/Tigers are endangered—form–meaning mapping varies. L2 predictions: Article-less L1s overuse the for specificity or familiarity, underuse a in novel but non-specific contexts; difficulty with generic readings. Micro-demo: Two-sentence contexts that force definite vs. indefinite vs. specific readings; students pick the felicitous article. 3) Quantifier scope & ambiguity resolution # Key notes: Scope options: A student read every book (∃ > ∀ vs. ∀ > ∃). Diagnostics: picture verification, TVJT with explicit contexts, or continuation tasks. L2 predictions: Preference for surface scope early; inverse scope access depends on L1, proficiency, and processing load. Think–pair–share: Draft one context sentence that forces inverse scope for A reviewer read every paper, then test with a minimal prompt. Pacing: ~12 min per mini-topic + ~9 min discussion.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Build a minimal, diagnostic task for one interface domain.
Choose ONE and complete the template:
A. Telicity via object quantization
Materials: Triplets (telic vs. atelic), e.g., eat an apple / eat apples / eat three apples. Task: TVJT with animated clips (bounded/unbounded); or acceptability with aspectual adverbs (in an hour vs. for an hour). Prediction: Learners with article-less/mass-preference L1s will over-accept atelic + in an hour and under-accept telic + in an hour early on. B. Article semantics (definite/specific/generic)
Materials: Two-sentence contexts fixing discourse status (unique/familiar, novel-specific, generic). Task: Contexted AJT (choose the/a/∅), plus a short explanation prompt. Prediction: Overuse of the in novel-specific contexts; instability in generic mappings (Tigers are… vs. The tiger is…). C. Quantifier scope
Materials: Contexts that force inverse scope; test sentences with two quantifiers. Task: TVJT with pictures/scenarios; optional SPR for online costs at disambiguation. Prediction: Preference for surface scope; inverse scope improves with proficiency and supportive contexts. Deliverable: 3-line prereg—hypothesis, primary DV (accuracy/TVJ acceptances, RTs), and falsifier.
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette
Group A (Mandarin L1 → English): unstable article choices in novel-specific contexts; overuse of the. Group B (Russian L1 → English): near-native telicity with measure phrases but difficulty with generic readings; surface-biased scope preferences. Questions:
Which patterns suggest feature-mapping problems (DP) vs. composition problems (telicity) vs. processing preferences (scope)? What context manipulation would make the target meaning diagnostic for each group? Propose one classroom intervention (e.g., article choice with discourse cards; telicity training via in/for an hour diagnostics; scope paraphrase/verification drills). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Why does eat an apple tend to be telic while eat apples is atelic? Give a context where a is correct but the is infelicitous. Provide a sentence with a scope ambiguity and name its two readings. How can aspectual adverbs diagnose telicity? What outcome suggests a processing (not representational) limitation for scope? 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 10) # In ~300 words, choose one domain (telicity, articles, or scope). (a) State a claim, (b) derive a prediction keyed to a specific context manipulation, (c) select one task + DV (TVJT, AJT, SPR), and (d) specify a falsifier for your preferred account.
🧭 Preview of Week 10 # We extend to syntax–discourse & semantics–pragmatics interfaces (topic/focus, anaphora, implicatures): how discourse structure and pragmatic inferences interact with grammar in L2.

title: Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces
content:
Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 11.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # How information structure (topic/focus) and prosody/word order interact, and why mappings differ across languages. Why pronoun interpretation (null vs. overt, topic continuity/shift) and anaphora resolution are challenging external-interface phenomena. How pragmatic inferences (e.g., scalar implicatures) arise and why they can be delayed or optional in L2 processing. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Define topic, focus, and givenness, and explain how languages encode them (prosody, particles, word order, clefts). Describe how subject expression and pronoun resolution depend on syntactic and discourse cues, and derive L1-specific predictions. Explain scalar implicature computation (e.g., some → not all) and state conditions that favor or suppress it. Design a compact contexted task that elicits interface-sensitive judgments or online processing signatures. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 11 (focus: topic/focus & prosody/word order; overt vs. null pronouns and discourse; scalar implicatures and other pragmatic inferences). Optional: Review Ch. 3 (processing) for methods used in online pragmatics, and Ch. 8–10 for connections to syntax and semantics. Guiding questions:
When does a language mark focus with prosody alone vs. with syntax (word order/clefts) or particles (e.g., only/even)? In null-subject languages, when is an overt pronoun preferred, and what does that mean for L2 learners’ choices? What contexts trigger a scalar implicature, and how can we encourage/expose it experimentally? 🧠 Key terms # information structure; topic; focus; givenness; contrastive focus; clefting; focus particles; prosody/intonation; subject expression; null vs. overt pronoun; anaphora resolution; discourse prominence; scalar implicature; implicature cancellation; contexted acceptability; discourse completion; TVJT; visual-world eye-tracking.
🔍 Core ideas # External interfaces are fragile: Mappings between grammar and discourse/pragmatics (topic continuity, focus interpretation, implicatures) show optional or delayed behavior in L2, even when core syntax/semantics are in place. Encoding focus/topic varies by language: English often relies on prosody and clefts; many languages also use word order or particles. L2 learners must learn which cue does the heavy lifting. Subject expression & pronouns: In null-subject languages, null often signals topic continuity; overt can mark topic shift/emphasis. L2 learners may overuse overt pronouns or omit required overt subjects depending on L1. Scalar implicatures (SIs): Inferences like some → not all are context-sensitive and can be resource-demanding; L2ers often compute SIs less or later unless context licenses them strongly. 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Information structure: topic, focus, and encoding strategies # Key notes: Topic = what the sentence is about; focus = new/contrastive information. Languages differ: prosodic focus (pitch accent) vs. syntactic (clefts, fronting) vs. particles (only/even). Prediction: L2ers transfer L1-preferred cue (prosody/syntax/particle) → early mis-matches in L2. Class spark: Provide 4 short contexts; students pick among plain SVO, cleft (It is X that…), or focus particle (only X) for best fit. 2) Pronoun interpretation & subject expression at the discourse interface # Key notes: Null vs. overt subject pronoun choice tracks topic continuity vs. shift in many pro-drop languages. L2 predictions: From a pro-drop L1 → English: omission errors; From a non-pro-drop L1 → Spanish/Italian: overuse of overt pronouns in topic-continuity contexts. Micro-demo: Two-sentence mini-discourses that force continuity vs. shift; learners choose null/overt (or pronoun vs. name) and justify. 3) Scalar implicatures and pragmatic computation # Key notes: SIs arise when a stronger alternative exists (all > some); speakers choose the weaker term to implicate the stronger is false. Triggered by context and task; can be cancelled (Some, maybe all). Prediction: L2ers accept literal readings more; SI rates go up with supportive contexts and time. Think–pair–share: Craft a one-line context that forces an SI for some; then write an explicit cancellation continuation. Pacing: ~12 minutes per subtopic + ~9 minutes guided discussion.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: Build a contexted test for one interface phenomenon.
Choose ONE and complete the template.
A. Topic/focus mapping
Materials: Contexts that require contrastive focus vs. broad focus. Task: Contexted acceptability comparing plain SVO vs. cleft vs. focus particle; optional prosody track (audio with/without focal accent). Prediction: L2ers overuse the L1-preferred device and show lower acceptability when the L2-preferred cue is missing. B. Pronoun resolution / subject expression
Materials: Two-sentence discourses manipulating topic continuity vs. shift. Task: Discourse completion (choose form: null/overt/name) + visual-world eye-tracking (pronoun resolution to antecedent). Prediction: From non-pro-drop L1 → pro-drop L2: overuse overt subjects in continuity; eye-tracking shows delayed fixation to discourse-topical referent for null pronouns. C. Scalar implicature
Materials: Contexts biasing not-all vs. allowing literal truth. Task: TVJT (true/false/“infelicitous”) + optional self-paced reading at the implicature trigger and continuation. Prediction: Lower SI endorsement overall; increased SI with supportive contexts or slower tasks. Deliverable: 3-line prereg—hypothesis, primary DV (acceptability, choice, RTs/fixations), and falsifier.
🧩 In-class application (Session 3, 45 min) # Case vignette
Group A (English L1 → Spanish L2): frequent overt subjects in topic-continuity contexts; near-native case marking elsewhere. Group B (Mandarin L1 → English L2): prefers clefts or focus particles over prosodic focus; literal bias on some. Questions:
Which patterns indicate interface mapping issues vs. processing preferences? What context manipulation would make the target interpretation diagnostic (e.g., add explicit contrast/topic tracking)? Propose one instructional task per group (e.g., discourse cards guiding pronoun choice; prosody training with minimal pairs; SI drills using alternatives lists). ✅ Self-check (answers hidden) # Define topic vs. focus and give one encoding strategy for each. In a pro-drop language, when is an overt subject pronoun preferred? What is a scalar implicature for some and how can it be cancelled? Give one L1-transfer prediction for topic/focus realization. Name one online method for pronoun resolution and its diagnostic measure. 📝 Weekly analytical note (due before Week 11) # In ~300 words, pick one domain (topic/focus, pronoun interpretation, or scalar implicature). (a) State a claim with an L1-based prediction, (b) design one contexted task with a clear DV, and (c) specify a result that would falsify your preferred account (e.g., native-like choices offline but delayed online).
🧭 Preview of Week 11 # Next: L2 processing & methods — a toolkit for grammaticality judgments, self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and ERP, with design pitfalls and effect-size/power considerations.

title: Week 11 — L2 Processing & Experimental Methods
content:
Week 11 — L2 Processing & Experimental Methods # Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 12.
⭐ Overview (for preview) # A compact toolkit for studying L2 processing: what offline vs. online methods measure and when to use them. How to align theoretical claims with diagnostic tasks, dependent variables, and analysis plans. Common design pitfalls (speed–accuracy tradeoff, item effects, underpowered samples) and how to avoid them. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of this week you should be able to:
Map a theory claim to an appropriate method (GJT/AJT, SPR, eye-tracking, ERP) and DV. Define key online signatures (e.g., first-pass vs. regression-path times; N400/P600 windows) and what they imply. Draft a minimal, well-controlled design (counterbalancing, fillers, regions/time-windows, exclusions). Specify an analysis plan (effect size, mixed-effects modeling basics, power/pre-registration) with a clear falsifier. 📖 Reading (do before Session 1) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Ch. 12 (overview of methods for L2 processing; morphology/syntax effects; individual differences). Optional: Revisit Ch. 3 for processing fundamentals to connect constructs to measures. Guiding questions:
What new insight does an online method offer beyond offline accuracy? For your research interest (e.g., agreement, article semantics, scope), which task + DV is most diagnostic and why? 🧠 Key terms # offline vs. online; (timed) grammaticality/acceptability judgment (GJT/AJT); self-paced reading (SPR); region of interest (ROI); spillover; eye-tracking (first fixation, first-pass/gaze, regression-path, total time, skipping); ERP (baseline, time window, N400, LAN, P600); randomization, counterbalancing, Latin square; fillers; speed–accuracy tradeoff; response bias; mixed-effects models; random intercepts/slopes; effect size; power; preregistration; exclusion criteria.
🔍 Core ideas # Match claim ↔ measure: Processing claims require time-course measures; competence claims require untimed judgments/comprehension—ideally use both. Signature patterns: SPR: region-locked slowdowns at the critical ROI (plus spillover). Eye-tracking: early first-pass differences vs. later regression-path/total time; skipping rates reflect predictability. ERP: N400 (lexical/semantic integration), P600 (syntactic reanalysis/morpho-syntax), sometimes LAN (early morpho-syntax). Design hygiene: Control lexical frequency/length, avoid item confounds, counterbalance lists, add fillers, and include comprehension checks to maintain task engagement. Analysis basics: Report effect sizes, use mixed-effects models with participants/items as random factors, predefine exclusions (e.g., <60% comprehension, RT outliers), and consider power (planned N). 🗂️ Mini-lecture outline (Session 1, 45 min) # 1) Choosing the right method & DV # Key notes: Untimed AJT/GJT → competence judgments; Timed GJT → adds processing pressure. SPR → linear text, precise ROI comparisons; Eye-tracking → natural reading with multiple measures; ERP → millisecond-level neural signatures. Avoid speed–accuracy tradeoff and response bias (include foils, practice, and comprehension probes). Class spark: Given a claim (“L2 readers compute agreement but more slowly”), students pick one method + one DV and justify. 2) Online signatures & interpretation # Key notes: SPR: establish pre-critical baseline, identify critical and spillover regions. Eye-tracking: what first-pass, regression-path, total time, and skipping each index. ERP: define baseline, time-windows (e.g., 300–500 ms N400; 500–800 ms P600); control artifacts and trial counts. Micro-demo: Annotate a sample sentence with ROIs/time-windows; predict where effects should appear. 3) Design hygiene & analysis plan # Key notes: Stimuli: balance lexical properties, avoid unintended cues; Latin-square lists to distribute conditions. Fillers: mix structures to reduce strategy. Stats: mixed-effects (participants/items), pre-registered contrasts, effect size, power (pilot or simulation). Exclusions: comprehension accuracy threshold; RT trimming rules; ERP artifact criteria. Think–pair–share: Identify one threat to validity in a sample design and propose a fix. Pacing: ~12 min each mini-topic + ~9 min Q&A fits 45 minutes.
🧪 Methods micro-lab (Session 2, 45 min) # Goal: From claim → materials → DV → analysis (compact prereg sheet).
Choose ONE template and fill it in:
A. Agreement attraction (SPR)
Hypothesis: L2 readers represent agreement but suffer similarity-based interference. Materials: Sentences like “The key to the cabinets … is/are …” with match/mismatch conditions. DV: RT at verb region (+ spillover). Analysis: Mixed-effects on logRTs; fixed effects = Match × Grammaticality, random intercepts/items; define outlier trimming. Falsifier: No mismatch cost at the verb region despite adequate power. B. Wh-dependency (Eye-tracking)
Hypothesis: L2 readers build filler–gap dependencies but incur larger reanalysis costs. Materials: Grammatical vs. island violations; gap/disambiguation region marked. DV: Regression-path time at disambiguation; first-pass at gap. Analysis: Mixed-effects per measure; accuracy screen on comprehension Qs. Falsifier: Equal regression-path times across grammatical vs. island conditions. C. Semantic vs. morpho-syntactic violations (ERP)
Hypothesis: L2 shows N400 to semantic anomalies, P600 to morpho-syntactic ones, with possible latency differences. Materials: Minimal pairs (semantic violation vs. agreement violation vs. control). DV: Mean amplitude in 300–500 ms (N400) and 500–800 ms (P600) windows at preselected electrodes. Analysis: Repeated-measures/mixed models; artifact rejection rules; minimum trials per condition. Falsifier: Absence of condition effects with sufficient clean trials and power. Deliverable: 5 bullet prereg—Hypothesis, Materials, DV(s), Exclusions, Model/Contrasts.
